module.js_secrets.checks: Reads the site's scripts and the page's inline scripts: looks for 16 kinds of secrets (AWS, Stripe, GitHub, Slack keys, JWT, private key, password…) with masked values, and lists API endpoints and external APIs.
module.js_secrets.fix:
Immediately revoke each reported secret (AWS key, Stripe secret key, GitHub or Slack token, SendGrid, Mailgun or Twilio key, password, private key) in the console of the service concerned, then create a new one. Deleting the JavaScript file is not enough: the secret may have been copied, cached or archived.
Review the service's audit, access and billing logs since the date the file was published to spot fraudulent use (sending, data access, abnormal costs). If personal data may have been read, assess your notification obligation.
Remove the secret from the code delivered to the browser: a secret must never appear in public JavaScript. Move the call to a server-side service that keeps the key in an environment variable or a secrets manager, and send the browser only the result.
Keys designed to be public (Stripe publishable key `pk_live`, Firebase configuration, a browser Google key) are not revoked: restrict them (allowed domains, allowed APIs, Firebase security rules) so they cannot be abused.
Purge the copies: repository history (for example with `git filter-repo`), build artifacts, CDN and browser caches; then redeploy the site.
Do not publish source maps (`.map`) in production: turn off their generation (`devtool: false` with webpack, `build.sourcemap: false` with Vite) or block access to them on the server (snippet).
Protect the sensitive endpoints cited in the JavaScript (`/admin`, `/debug`, `/actuator`, `/swagger`, `/api-docs`, `/graphiql`, `/console`): mandatory authentication, access limited to an internal network or a VPN, API documentation and debugging switched off in production.
Prevent a repeat by scanning for secrets before each release (gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning), then run the scan again.
module.js_secrets.title: JavaScript secrets
module.js_secrets.why: A secret published in JavaScript is readable by everyone: it must be revoked immediately. The listed API endpoints map what an attacker can query.
